name: Marco Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day of work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Marco, 43. I have a music bachelor’s and play drums for live theatre shows, make short rhythm beds, meaning backing drum beats, for local adverts, and teach five pupils at a rehearsal studio. I’ve done it for years and I’m a reliable, ordinary session player rather than the drummer everybody flies in. I like getting a room of actors to land on the same beat; I dislike an advert client calling a paid revision a tiny favour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that income fit life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a dental practice, and our two children are in school. We pay a mortgage, earn well for our line of work and have about ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other music jobs nearby, though I would still need an actual vacancy. I use AI now and then to sort dates, but I check every call against the theatre schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that a quicker booking list is welcome if show fees are still agreed before rehearsal. A machine cannot ask the drummer to come in softer after a singer loses the beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is manageable with two incomes and ten months saved. I would still guard the revision fee on advert beds, because a client can ask for unpaid changes without any new AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the theatre shows, five pupils and advert sessions this season. This week I’d ask the studio to confirm paid teaching hours and put one cleared advert fee into our mortgage reserve whenever a session pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work under a small change. The booking system can be annoying, but we do not need to raid savings for a late invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an unpaid revision look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop once asked for a new drum ending after approving the first cut. I sent a price before opening the session again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you already use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use a tool to sort gig dates. I do not ask it to judge a pupil’s timing or put their recording online.

say: I would welcome a faster **booking list** with agreed show fees.
I would tell actors that a **live drummer** can adjust to a singer.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and two incomes cover ordinary delays.
An unpaid **advert revision** still matters to my fee.
do: Keep **theatre shows**, five pupils and advert sessions this season.
Confirm paid **teaching hours** and save one cleared advert fee when sessions pay.
feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work covers the mortgage and routine delays.
S0.quote: A machine cannot ask the drummer to come in softer after a singer loses the beat.
fieldNote: His **higher pay** and ten-month reserve make a late invoice manageable alongside his partner’s regular dental-practice income.
His occasional **AI use** sorts dates, not a pupil’s playing.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre shows, five pupils and advert sessions this season
Save one cleared advert fee in mortgage reserve whenever sessions pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the musicians’ association that generated rhythm beds will make a small advert budget look smaller still. I would ask for a minimum session fee and written limits on reusing our stems, the separate recorded instrument parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert beds bring about a third of my music pay. If clients replace them, the theatre and pupils remain, but our mortgage reserve stops growing and I may lose a large part of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI timing-check feature on drum files I own, compare its marks with my ears and the theatre call, and keep pupil recordings out of it. In the first year, if advert orders fall, I’d bring paid invoices to the association for a reuse clause and stop booking the extra studio day when it has no paid session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a sustained third of my pay going missing. Ten months saved would let us choose carefully, but savings do not invoice a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the timing feature actually teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn to spot where its beat markers drift on a live take. Date sorting does not tell me that, and I would test it only on my own tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which work would disappear first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first loss would be a thirty-second drum bed for a shop advert. Two such beds pay our mortgage service charge for a month.

say: I would seek **minimum session fees** and reuse limits through the association.
I would warn that **generated rhythm beds** can replace paid advert work.
think: Advert beds supply about **one third** of my music income.
Losing those fees would halt **reserve growth** even while live shows continue.
do: Learn new **AI timing checks** on owned drum files this month; compare marks with my ears and theatre call, excluding pupils.
Ask the **association** for reuse terms if adverts fall; cancel empty studio days.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a third of my music income.
S1.quote: Ten months saved would let us choose carefully, but savings do not invoice a client.
fieldNote: His new **AI learning** concerns beat markers on owned tracks, beyond occasional date sorting.
A large **advert share** supports association action and cuts to empty studio days.

steps.text: Learn AI timing checks on owned drums; compare marks with ears and theatre call, excluding pupils
Ask musicians’ association for minimum session fees and reuse terms if advert orders fall
Cancel extra studio day in first year if advert orders fall and no session pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AGI by 2028 can make rhythm beds and booking plans cheaply, while robots able to play a live kit arrive around 2031. I would ask the theatre for its paid dates rather than guess how long live shows last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert beds to go first, taking a third of my music pay. Ten months saved and several local employers help, but a school vacancy is not mine until I have an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get written theatre dates and keep the five pupils on their current paid hours. In the first year after 2028, if advert orders stop, I’d end the extra studio day at renewal and apply for an advertised school percussion post only if the school accepts my music degree and experience and its written net wage covers travel and confirmed childcare; I’d keep the theatre and pupils until a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, because a lost third is a large hole even with savings. I would not wake the children with a crisis story before we have a real pay figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower salary to get a school timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare net pay after travel and childcare before giving up shows. A neat timetable cannot pay the mortgage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use your reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep it for a gap in fees, not use it to fund an unpaid trial job. If the school cannot state its pay in writing, I would keep the current bookings.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from live-playing robots around 2031.
I would ask the theatre for **paid dates** before trusting live work.
think: Advert losses could remove **one third** of my music pay.
A **ten-month reserve** buys time, not a school offer.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** until written offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
End **extra studio day** at renewal if 2028 advert orders stop.
Seek **advertised school post** if orders stop and credentials accepted; require written net wage covering travel and confirmed childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a large, likely loss to my own pay.
S2.quote: A neat timetable cannot pay the mortgage by itself.
fieldNote: His **advert exposure** reaches a full third of music income before robots can play in 2031.
A school move requires **accepted credentials**, written net pay and confirmed childcare.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre shows and five pupils until written school offer
End extra studio day at renewal if 2028 advert orders stop
Seek advertised school post if 2028 orders stop, credentials accepted, written net wage covers travel/childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the association that five years gives players time to negotiate reuse and prove that live rhythm teaching sells. Thinking AGI would reach advert beds around 2031, and capable robot drummers around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could replace part of the advert income with an evening ensemble, but I would need paid adults rather than compliments. My partner’s practice closes late twice a week, so pickup must be settled first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I’d ask an independent arts centre for a free room and offer a six-week adult drum circle only if nine people prepay enough to cover my teaching and setup time and my partner confirms pickup. In the first year after 2031 I’d repeat it only if nine still pay enough for my time, the room remains free and pickup is covered; I’d keep theatre shows while they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about those advert fees, but I have time to find out whether the circle really earns. A full room on a poster is not a paid room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as setup time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have to tune and move the drums before anyone arrives. Nine payments need to cover that hour as well as the six lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only seven people pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund the seven and keep teaching my existing pupils. I would not use the reserve to make an empty arts centre look busy.

say: I would seek **recording rights** before 2031 through the association.
I would test a **paid drum circle** rather than count expressions of interest.
think: A **nine-person group** could replace some advert fees only if it pays for setup.
My partner’s late shifts make **pickup** a real limit.
do: Ask the arts centre for a **free room** next term; start only with nine prepayments covering teaching and setup and confirmed pickup.
Repeat the **circle** after 2031 only if nine cover teaching and setup, room free and pickup covered; keep paid shows.
feel: I feel **anxious** about advert pay despite time to test the circle.
S3.quote: A full room on a poster is not a paid room.
fieldNote: His **circle price** must cover moving drums and setup before teaching starts, without using family savings.
He keeps **paid theatre shows** and does not subsidise the trial from savings.

steps.text: Start six-week circle with free arts-centre room, nine prepayments covering teaching/setup and pickup confirmed
Repeat circle after 2031 only if nine cover teaching/setup, room free and pickup covered
Keep paid theatre shows while bookings continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that ten years is time to learn the price of a session and why it belongs in writing. Thinking AGI comes around 2036 and robot drummers around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still play the theatre, and our reserve makes the next few years manageable. Yet the advert work could go before my hands are threatened, and the mortgage will still want real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the theatre and five pupils and save one cleared advert fee after each month’s mortgage payment. Over the decade I’d keep the adult circle only with a free room, nine prepayments covering my teaching and setup, and confirmed pickup; in the first year after 2036, if advert income ends, I’d seek an advertised school percussion role only if my credentials are accepted and the written net offer covers travel and childcare, while keeping paid shows until an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about work in a decade, not frightened about the present month. Time lets me check a job’s pay before I leave a stage that still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for a new kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the school’s posted requirements before buying any course. My music degree may be enough, and I will not spend tuition on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you tell your children about music pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them a paid show invoice and the hours behind it. A performance is not just the hour when the audience claps.

say: I would distinguish **2036 thinking AGI** from robot drummers around 2039.
I would explain **session pay** to my children in writing.
think: At **53**, the theatre might still pay while advert work changes.
Our **reserve** allows deliberate decisions, not a guarantee of future gigs.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** this year; save cleared advert fees after mortgage payments.
Keep the **adult circle** only with free room, nine payments covering teaching/setup and confirmed pickup.
Seek **advertised school role** after 2036 if adverts end, credentials accepted, written net offer covers travel/childcare; keep paid shows until offer.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant work while current mortgage payments are manageable.
S4.quote: A performance is not just the hour when the audience claps.
fieldNote: He builds **reserve money** from cleared fees rather than anticipated bookings.
A later **school move** depends on real vacancy, accepted credentials, written pay and continued shows until offer.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre shows and five pupils this year and until written school offer
Save one cleared advert fee after each mortgage payment while sessions pay
Keep circle after 2036 only with free room, nine prepayments covering teaching/setup and pickup
Seek advertised school role if post-2036 adverts end, credentials accepted, written net offer covers travel/childcare

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the advert beds are a third of my music pay and could end before robots touch a drum. Paid theatre dates, reuse limits through the association and an actual school vacancy with written net pay and workable childcare would help. I would keep current pupils until that offer is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a generated rhythm bed still uses a player’s old recordings. My drum-recording invoice is small, but the recording can earn for someone else for years.

headlineQuote: My drum-recording invoice is small, but the recording can earn for someone else for years.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old drummer** with a music bachelor’s, theatre work, advert sessions and five pupils.
His **higher pay**, partner’s dental-practice work, mortgage and ten-month reserve support two school-age children.
He uses **AI occasionally** for dates and newly learns timing checks only on owned tracks.
Fast AGI threatens **advert beds** before robot drummers; he tests prepaid group teaching and weighs an actual school role.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could erase advert beds worth a third of music pay.
whatWouldHelp: Written **theatre dates** and association reuse limits would protect paid work.
A real **school vacancy** with accepted credentials, written net pay and childcare coverage would enable a move.
